meta.title: The work — Nagy Habib
meta.description: The body of work of Professor Nagy Habib: hepatobiliary surgery, the Habib radiofrequency instruments and the companies behind them, and translational research in liver disease.

sections.label: The work
sections.quote: Three sides of <t>one body of work.</t>
sections.sub: The surgery, the instruments and companies that came out of it, and the research that keeps feeding both.

sections.label: Firsts
sections.title: A record <t>of firsts.</t>
sections.lede: Each with its year and the paper that reported it.
items: 1993. The first living-related liver transplant in Africa and the Middle East. International Surgery, 1993.
2001. The first clinical trial of an engineered adenovirus against liver cancer. Human Gene Therapy, 2001.
2002. Liver resection by radiofrequency, sealing the tissue before the cut. Annals of Surgery, 2002.
2006. Patients’ own bone-marrow stem cells for liver insufficiency, among the first such trials in the West. Stem Cells, 2006.
2008. Hydrodynamic gene delivery to a single segment of the human liver. Cancer Gene Therapy, 2008.
2020. The first small activating RNA drug given to patients. Clinical Cancer Research, 2020.

sections.label: In detail
sections.title: The surgery, the instruments, <t>the companies.</t>
sections.lede: As listed by Imperial College London, Boston Scientific and the companies themselves.

groups.label: Surgery
names: Liver, pancreatic and biliary surgery at Hammersmith Hospital, as Professor of Hepatobiliary Surgery at Imperial College London since 2003
Radiofrequency-assisted, near-bloodless liver resection, the technique known as Habib’s resection
First living-related liver transplant in Africa and the Middle East, 1993

groups.label: Instruments
names: Habib 4X: bipolar radiofrequency resection for liver and pancreas, launched in 2005 with Imperial’s Department of Engineering, FDA-cleared and CE-marked; licensed to Rita Medical, now AngioDynamics; some 70,000 units sold by 2018
Habib EndoHPB: an endoscopic bipolar radiofrequency probe for tumours that block the bile duct; with EMcision, acquired by Boston Scientific on 5 March 2018

groups.label: Companies
names: EMcision — surgical devices; a spin-out from Imperial College London; acquired by Boston Scientific, 2018
MiNA Therapeutics — small activating RNA; co-founded, with Robert Habib as founding Chief Executive since 2013
OmniCyte, Medeva and Bioenvision — as listed in his own account of the companies he co-founded

groups.label: Research
names: Adenovirus and plasmid gene therapy for liver cancer; plasmid gene therapy by hydrodynamic delivery
Autologous bone-marrow and CD34+ stem cells for liver insufficiency
Small activating RNA, from the preclinical work on CEBPA to the first-in-human trial of MTL-CEBPA
Centre for Advanced Therapeutics, Imperial College London

sections.label: Through MiNA Therapeutics
sections.sub: Co-founded with Robert Habib, its founding Chief Executive since 2013. Small activating RNA raises the activity of a gene instead of silencing it; MTL-CEBPA, designed to restore C/EBP-α in the liver, was the first drug of its kind given to patients, in a phase I trial published in 2020. Professor Habib serves on the company’s Scientific Advisory Board.
